1.goal: To open the lesson on something she already has — her own last trip — and to say once where the hour ends.
1.interaction: T–S, open questions. She may answer in Portuguese.
run: Ask whether she managed to open the pre-class, and whether anything in it was unclear.
Say, once, what today is: she reads one hotel booking and then says four sentences in English, out loud, to you.
Ask the question on screen — where she went on her last trip. One answer is enough.
Say the name of the place back in English so she hears it once, and move on.
exact: About the pre-class: "Did you open the pre-class? Was anything hard?"
What today is: "Today you read one hotel booking. Then you say four sentences in English, out loud."
If nothing comes, the two options: "Inside Brazil, or outside Brazil?"
1.expected: One place, and a sentence or two about it. Portuguese is fine at this point.
1.support: If nothing comes, offer two options and let her choose one. Choosing is also answering.
1.challenge: If she answers easily, ask who she traveled with and take that answer too.
1.monitoring: Whether she starts talking at all, and in which language. This is the baseline of the cycle.
1.evidence: Where she went last, and whether the pre-class reached her.
1.transition: Move on when she has named a place and heard what today is.

2.goal: To set the scene the lesson turns on, and to separate what the desk needs to hear from what it does not.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief and choosing from the list on screen.
run: Read the brief with her, slowly.
Read the seven items under the question with her and ask which ones the person at the desk needs to hear. Three of them do not belong to a booking.
Take her choices without correcting one by one; confirm the four at the end.
exact: The question, item by item: "Your job — does the desk need that?"
Closing the four: "So: your name, the city, the dates, and what is included."
2.expected: Your name, the city, the dates, what is included. Your job, the weather today and your favorite food are the three that do not belong.
2.support: If she is unsure about an item, ask whether that information would be written on the paper itself.
2.challenge: Ask which of the four the desk asks for first.
2.monitoring: Whether she rejects the three that do not belong, or accepts the whole list.
2.evidence: How many of the four she already recognizes before reading anything.
2.transition: Move on when the four are named and she knows what she is about to read.

3.goal: To have her risk a guess about what is in a booking, before she sees one.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Portuguese accepted.
run: Read the three questions on screen out loud with her.
Take one guess on each. Do not confirm and do not correct — these are hypotheses.
If she risks nothing, offer two options and ask her to choose.
exact: The two options: "A name and a date, or a name and a price?"
After the guess: "Good. That is your guess. Now we look."
3.expected: Three guesses, however rough. Name and dates usually come up; the fourth thing usually does not.
3.support: Offer two and let her choose. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask which of the four she thinks the hotel checks first, and why.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess at all, or waits to be told the right answer.
3.evidence: Whether she guesses without being sure.
3.transition: Move on when she has answered all three, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read a whole document once, without a dictionary, and say what it is and who it is for.
4.interaction: S alone for two minutes, then T–S.
run: Read the question at the top with her first, so she reads with something to look for.
Two minutes in silence. No dictionary, and no stopping on a word.
Then take the answer: what this paper is, and who it is for. The paper does not name itself — saying what it is IS the task.
If she stops on a word, give her the word and let her keep going.
exact: If she is stuck on a word, give it plainly: "That word is guest — it is hóspede. Keep going."
4.expected: It is a hotel booking, and it is hers — her name is on it. Two facts, not a summary.
4.support: If she starts translating line by line, cover everything except the first two lines and ask again.
4.challenge: Ask which line she would look at first if she were standing at the desk.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads the whole thing, or stops at the first word she does not know.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what the paper is and who it is for.

5.goal: To separate what the paper says from what she assumed it said.
5.interaction: S answers on screen, T checks with her.
run: The instruction and the booking are both on this screen — she does not have to hold anything in her head.
She answers yes or no for each of the six sentences, then presses Check and you go through it together.
Discuss only the ones she got wrong. The button becomes Redo if she wants to run it again.
5.expected: Four yes and two no. The two that are not in the paper are the pool and the price.
5.support: If she hesitates, ask her to point at the line that says it. If she cannot point at it, the answer is no.
5.challenge: Ask how many nights the booking is for. It is the one thing the paper does not say in words, and the one the hotel will ask.
5.monitoring: This is where her first mistake of the lesson is most likely. Take it as normal, out loud, in one sentence, and carry on.
5.evidence: Which of the six she missed, and whether she could point at the line afterwards.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked.

6.goal: For her to see, herself, the difference between one word and a whole sentence.
6.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: Four lines on screen; she marks the two that are whole sentences and presses Check.
Then ask, in Portuguese if you need to: which of them does a person at a desk understand better?
Do not name any grammar rule today. The verb to be belongs to lesson 3, and it arrives after she has already used it.
6.expected: I am in Lisbon. and It is from 14 October to 18 October. are the two whole sentences.
6.support: If she cannot say why, read both versions out loud yourself and ask which one sounds like an answer.
6.challenge: Ask her to turn the other two into whole sentences.
6.monitoring: Whether she names the difference herself, or waits for you to name it.
6.evidence: Whether she can state the difference between a word and a sentence in her own words.
6.transition: Move on when she has said the difference.

7.goal: To get the four sentences said out loud, many times, until they come out whole.
7.interaction: T says the cue word, S gives back the whole sentence. In rounds, fast.
run: The four cue words are in the box at the top, out of order; the four openings are listed below it.
Say one cue; she finds the opening that fits and gives back the whole sentence. Then again out of order, then again faster.
Correct gently and immediately, with no explanation.
This is the longest stage of the lesson: the repetition here is what makes the sentence exist in stage 7.
exact: The cues, one at a time: "Breakfast." / "Fourteen to eighteen October." / "Vanessa." / "Lisbon."
If only one word comes back, give the opening and nothing more: "My…" / "I am…" / "It is…" / "Breakfast…"
7.expected: My name is Vanessa. · I am in Lisbon. · It is from 14 October to 18 October. · Breakfast is included.
7.support: If only one word comes back, give the first word of the opening and wait. Do not finish the sentence for her.
7.challenge: Give two cues at once and ask for both sentences in a row.
7.monitoring: Whether the sentence comes out whole or in single words, and whether she translates before speaking.
7.evidence: How many rounds it took until the four came out whole twice in a row.
7.transition: Move on when the four have come out whole twice in a row.

8.goal: For her to say the four sentences to another person, live, with nothing to read.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are at the hotel desk; she has just arrived.
run: The four cues are on screen — they say WHAT to say, never how. Read them with her once before you open the desk.
The booking is not on screen: this stage measures what survives without the paper. If she blocks, press Show the booking, let her look, and close it again.
Open the desk yourself and wait: greet her and ask for her name.
Let her say the four. Do not correct anything during the role-play.
If she stops, give the first word of the sentence and nothing more.
exact: Opening the desk: "Good afternoon. Welcome to Hotel Marina. What is your name, please?"
Then one at a time: "And where are you now?" / "And when is your booking?" / "And what is included?"
If she stops, the first word and nothing else: "My…" / "I am…" / "It is…"
At the end: "That is the first time you have spoken English here. Four sentences, on day one."
8.expected: The four sentences, out loud, in any order. Whole sentences count; single words do not.
8.support: Give the first word of the opening and wait. Do not finish the sentence for her. Show the booking is the last step, not the first: with it open she reads instead of speaking.
8.challenge: Ask one extra question she has the language for: "And the room?"
8.monitoring: How many of the four survive once the paper leaves the screen.
8.evidence: The first sample of her production in English — write down what she actually said, as she said it.
8.transition: Move on when the four have been said.

9.goal: To give back one thing that worked and one to build on, and then to ask for the same four sentences about a different booking.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields on screen together, then a short retask.
run: Fill the four fields with her, not about her: what worked, one point to improve, one sentence as she said it, and the same sentence made clearer.
One point, not two. Praise the whole sentence and not the correct word.
Then press Replay: the instruction and the second booking open below it. Ask for the same four sentences with the new details.
exact: Opening the retask: "Same four sentences. New hotel, new city, new dates. Ready?"
If the new dates block her, say them once for her to repeat: "Third of March to fifth of March."
9.expected: The same four sentences with Porto, 3 March and 5 March in place of Lisbon and October.
9.support: If the new dates block her, say them out loud once and let her repeat before she builds the sentence around them.
9.challenge: Ask for the four without looking at the second booking either.
9.monitoring: Whether changing the values breaks the sentence, or only slows it down.
9.evidence: Whether the sentence survives new content. That is what tells you it is a sentence and not a memorized line.
9.transition: Move on when the four have come out with the new details.

10.goal: To name what she did today, and to leave the next lesson already announced.
10.interaction: T–S. She ticks what she recognizes; the confidence row is hers.
run: She marks what she recognizes on screen. Each line and each point of the scale carries the Portuguese beside it, so read them in English and let her use the Portuguese only to confirm.
Do not argue with the confidence row.
Say what she did today, in full: she read a whole document in English and said four sentences without it, on the first day.

Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about a real booking of hers, one optional writing about another booking, and two free beginner resources.
Announce lesson 2 — the hotel desk: three short questions, and what to say when she does not understand.
exact: Saying what she did: "Today you read a document in English, and you said four sentences without it. On your first day."
10.expected: Some of the six items ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could do at a desk tomorrow.
10.challenge: Ask which of today's phrases she would use first on her next trip.
10.monitoring: Where she puts herself on the confidence row, against what she actually did in stage 7.
10.evidence: Her own confidence reading, and whether it matches what you saw. Fill in the post-lesson record before you close.
